messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel was 42 when he sought treatment, a married South Asian American man who had spent most of his adult life thinking of himself as careful, restrained, and dependable. He worked as a tax inspector, a job built on precision and routine, and before the accident he had taken pride in being the person who noticed details and prevented mistakes. The event that brought him to treatment had occurred months earlier during an ordinary drive home, after a long day of field visits. He had been moving through an intersection when he struck another car. The other driver was seriously injured. Ravi did not describe the crash as a blur so much as a sequence that broke apart in his mind. Certain instants were fixed with unnatural sharpness—the violent angle of the other vehicle after impact, the sight of damaged metal, the sound that came from the collision and from the injured person afterward—while the surrounding moments dropped away entirely. He would say that there were stretches he could not account for at all, as if whole sections of time had been cut out. What returned to him instead were fragments, with the sounds often arriving first in his head.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi found that the world no longer felt governed by the assumptions he had lived by. He had believed that if a person was responsible, followed rules, and tried to do right, terrible things could be prevented. After the crash, that certainty felt destroyed. He was left with the conviction that he had failed in the one obligation that mattered most in that moment: he should have protected another person, and he had not. More than guilt, there was humiliation. He felt marked by what had happened, permanently diminished by the fact that he was now the kind of man who had caused catastrophic harm. Even when others did not say this, he assumed it could be seen.

His memories did not settle into a coherent story. If his wife asked him what happened, or if anyone referenced the accident, he became tense before he said a word, because talking about it seemed to pull him toward the same broken pieces rather than a full account. He could hear in his mind the sounds from the scene, vivid enough that he sometimes stopped mid-sentence. At other times he became frustrated and confused by how much was missing. He knew there had been people coming toward the vehicles, voices, movement, but he could not line it up properly. The inconsistency itself disturbed him: one second was crystal clear and then there was nothing.

Ravi tried to manage this privately. He worked hard not to think about the crash at all, cutting off the images as soon as they began and pushing conversations away from anything related to it. If colleagues in the tax office mentioned traffic accidents, insurance claims, or even a news story involving a collision, he would become quiet or find a reason to leave the room. During field work, seeing cars that had been dented or left damaged at the side of the road could suddenly bring the image of the other vehicle back into his mind. He began altering driving routes when he could, not because he said roads were dangerous in a general sense, but because the sight of an obviously struck car felt unbearable. On some days this made him late or distracted, and he noticed himself checking out mentally during meetings after a drive.

Outside work, funerals and cemeteries became especially difficult. In his family and community, attending services for the dead or participating in mourning rituals had once been expected and meaningful. Now the sight of a cemetery or the atmosphere of a funeral stirred the same sense of catastrophe and moral exposure. He did not need the event to be connected to the crash; grief-related settings alone were enough to fill him with dread. He began finding excuses not to attend. This had consequences at home. His wife noticed that he withdrew from family obligations that previously mattered deeply to him, and Ravi felt ashamed of that too, though he could not explain it without feeling pulled back toward the accident.

Much of his private mental life became punishing. He would tell himself that he deserved to suffer because someone else had suffered far more. At times he tried to steady himself by thinking it could have been worse, that the other person had not died, that more people could have been hurt. But this never brought relief for long; it sounded to him like an attempt to escape what he had done. He returned instead to the idea that his suffering was appropriate, perhaps even necessary.

By the time he came for help, Ravi was exhausted by the effort of keeping the event out of mind and by the way it kept returning in pieces anyway. The immediate reason for seeking treatment was a recent conversation at work in which a coworker casually referred to a serious roadway collision, and Ravi abruptly heard the crash sounds in his head so vividly that he had to leave the office and sit alone in his car. He told himself afterward that he could no longer pretend this would pass on its own. What frightened him most was that this one event had rewritten who he was: a man who had failed to protect another person, who could not trust his own account of what happened, and who felt disgraced in settings that reminded him of injury or death. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not forgiveness so much as the ability to speak about the crash without feeling overwhelmed by the sounds and broken images, and to return to his work and family without carrying the same constant sense of humiliation.
